summary: Ozone's Aluula-framed 3-strut big air and kiteloop kite with a 16-point bridle. Designed to jump close to the Edge while looping more easily; V2 adds a 17m and splits canopy weight (55g up to 9m, 46g from 10m).
best_for: Big air riders who want Aluula lightness with a looping-friendly 3-strut feel

reviews.video_title: Big Air Kite Review 25 - 2026 Ozone Vortex Ultra X V2
reviews.excerpt: the new model was noticeably more powerful, had improved sheet and go lift, an improved sweet spot when coming off the water, and had slightly improved hang time
reviews.verdict: this kite is the logical and desirable upgrade from one of the already better kites on the market
reviews.summary: Jason found the V2 noticeably more powerful than the original Vortex, with better sheet-and-go lift and slightly more hangtime. It came within about 5–10% of the Evo D/LAB's boost while being more stable and easier to time. The trade-off is heavier steering and a fuller, more pulling loop, and it flew best on a wide, heavier low-V bar.
reviews.full_transcript: Hello and welcome to another plus size kite review where in this video I will be covering and comparing to the market the latest A Lula kite from Ozone, the new Vortex Ultra X V2. And I'll be looking at how it boosts, loops, and the confidence it will inspire for you to progress in your big air riding. If you have not seen it already, I'd highly recommend checking out the review I did on the original Vortex, one of our favorite kites of 2024 because I will be discussing it a lot in this review of course. If you are new to the channel, I would also recommend checking out some of my recent reviews on some of the best big air kites of the last year. And you could also check out my big air tier lists for a rundown of all the kites I've covered over the last few years as no doubt I will be referencing many of them too. And if there's any kites you find interesting from those, check out the reviews on my channel. A huge thanks go to Ozone and our local store here in New Zealand, the NZ Board Store for providing these demo kites. But as always, if you are US based, check them out from MACkiteboarding who provide me with a lot of my demos and a lot of the other gear you'll see in this review. You might also notice me riding a sexy new board in some of the clips in this review from Roda Boards in the Netherlands. I have recently been loving this board and will be dropping a review about it very soon. As usual, I will also be measuring my height and tricks with the Surfer app, our preferred method of progression tracking and kite comparisons for height. Check out my profile on Surfer to see all the various kites that I've been boosting with and how high I went on them. And if you haven't given it a go yourself, I'd highly recommend trying it out because not only does it give you a measure of your height, but it also allows you to compare your various tricks from board off to loops to rotations without being penalized for your body position. Uh which obviously is a great advantage especially when you're competing with your friends at your level to land new things at new heights. If you like these reviews, I do have a tips page that you can find a link in the description and all of your donations just go to wind chasing for future reviews. Now with all that out of the way, let's get on to this amazing kite. So with this review, I was lucky enough to test the V2 Vortex in two sizes, both a 9 m and a 12. So I will be describing my experiences on each of these kites and doing my best to compare them to other kites I've been flying in those sizes over the years. I was fortunate enough to get multiple sessions on both sizes and I was able to compare the 12 m back-to-back with my 12 m Evo D Lab that I've had for 3 years now, but is still performing wonderfully and has in that time remain remained to me what I consider the overall best 12 m kite I've ever flown. With the 9 m version of the Vortex, I was able to ride it with a wide variety of kites from recent Dacron kites I have reviews coming out for very soon to past favorites like the Cabrinha Nitro, which I still consider one of the best overall big air and kite loop progression kites on the market to of course some of the top Aluula kites I've been riding lately including the original Vortex, which was one of the top big air kites of 2024. I was particularly excited to get the opportunity to ride another 12 m as I don't get to test that size as often as I'd like. Um in the last few years, aside from my Evo D Labs that I've had since 2023, the only other 12s I've tested are my Sonic for which I'm going to also put out a review for sure very soon um as a foil kite and the two 12s provided by Harlem, the Thrive and Peak, both of which are great overall kites, particularly the Thrive in that size, but I was curious to know what a more recent Alula three-strut might offer. In the first session I got to ride either of these kites, I took out the 12 m in a fairly light 18 to 20 knots and was immediately very pleased with the overall light bar pressure, its low end, the general power of the kite, its lift and hang time. It reminded me a lot of my Evo 12 m in the best ways and until I rode them back to back, I was very confident that this kite was the closest comparison I've ridden thus far. The the key noticeable difference I found between riding the Vortex and the Evo back to back in the 12 m size was that the Evo was still a little bit more explosive and a little bit faster through the loops in contrast to the Vortex, which was more stable in the air and easier to control if you were looking to just sheet and go action. But this meant you had a little bit less maneuverability of the kite as it flew through the air. I would most attribute this to the eight-point bridle, which as I've mentioned in other Ozone reviews, can make more technical kite movements while airborne require a little bit more effort. Thus, a bit more challenging if you are not used to that style of flight. What I mean by that is that the kite is very stable, which means it wants to remain in its position a bit more, particularly as you are putting a lot of tension on the lines while airborne, thus making it easier to go for rotations and board offs if you have a parked kite above your head, but if you are looking to move the kite quickly through the air to do loops in different directions or sent jumps more aggressively, the timing will just be a little bit slower and you'll have to engage the bar a little bit more. If you've seen their reviews, I mentioned this characteristic with the Ozone Edge V T and Liquid Alpha, as they are both five-strut kites with the eight-point attachments, but thankfully, the Vortex is not nearly as stable or tricky to move around as they are. So, it's not a massive hindrance once you're used to the timing. When I swapped down to the 9-m size, I had my feelings validated because I was getting a very similar experience. And when we were lucky enough to ride the V2 9-m back-to-back with the Evo D-Lab, we once again found the Vortex more stable and easier to park above your head, yet the Evo was certainly more responsive, powerful, and explosive at getting you off the water. In another session, we were able to compare the two Vortex models back-to-back, and my friends and I all agreed that the new model was noticeably more powerful, had improved sheet and go lift, an improved sweet spot when coming off the water, and had slightly improved hang time, or at least appeared to because of the kite's better stability in the air. But, that did mean however, the steering pressure was a little bit heavier and the kite was ever so slightly slower to respond and get through kite loops. Mainly because it created a fuller, rounder loop with a little bit more pull and didn't pivot on itself quite as quickly as the previous model. But, I'll go into a little bit more detail about that when specifically talking about looping. I should of course add that when I had the opportunity to ride any of these kites, the three-strut Aluula kites back-to-back with the top Dacron kites, the difference was just night and day and so noticeable in terms of the improved low end particularly, but the lift and general power as well. It certainly made the parts of the days where the wind would drop back a little bit a lot more enjoyable to be on the kites with the Aluula. Where you could give an edge to the top looping-focused Dacron kites is for their light, tight rotating, easy looping motion that is more ideal for progressing loopers getting into their first loops. But, outside of this, the three-strut Aluula kites pretty much dominated everywhere else, which is just a reminder for me why I still feel overall in most kite sizes, Aluula works best on three-strut kites because of how much it gives you with increased wind range potential, versatility among disciplines, and just general power and lift in all those sizes. One other note before we get on to the categories is that you will notice me riding different bars during the testing as I also tried the Vortex on a high Y setup at one stage, which I actually discovered was a mistake as the kite just didn't feel quite as balanced as it did with the style of bar it was designed for. I usually tend to prefer the feel of high Y bars, but of course, that's with the kites that are designed to ride with it. Um particularly obviously as I discovered with this Vortex, it just felt uh a little bit off. Um the key takeaway from all of my bar testing was that this kite suited a wider, heavier bar like Ozone would make. Um and of the brands I rode, the Harlem worked pretty well. The Nav Pro also did as well, but my Trust bar unfortunately was just a little bit too light and not wide enough to get the leverage this kite preferred at least in these sizes. So, the differences particularly between the Evo and the Vortex were more noticeable, um but I'll go into those a little bit more later. So, now let's discuss the key attributes of the Vortex V2, and as always, let's start with boosting and hangtime. As you would expect, this is an area the kite excels at in relation to the bulk of the market. As I mentioned already, there are significant improvements to the general power over the previous iteration starting from low end going all the way up to top end um with potential boosting and hangtime. We rode each kite back-to-back with the V1 um despite it being very gusty and on and off wind, we both agreed there was a noticeable difference in our ability to both ride upwind, get through large surf as you can see here, and of course send it big. And the jumping statistics both for themselves with each of us consistently jumping higher on our surfer with the V2, not just for straight boosting, but we were able to get more consistently higher loops and everything we did just felt a little bit more powered. In comparison to the Evo, however, we were riding the older model of Evo in the 12-m size and the newer model Evo in the 9-m size. And in both cases, the Evos did have just a little bit more boosting potential and they were more explosive in general, uh particularly coming off the water. But the overall difference was small compared to the previous model. And in each session where they were being compared, that overall jump height on the top end were all within a meter of two of each other between the Evos and the Vortex V2 in sessions on the 12 and on the uh nine that sometimes eclipsed 30 knots. So, perhaps the difference was within maybe 5 to 10% difference from kite to kite with of course that slight advantage in general height going to the Evo. Where the Vortex would likely have some significant advantage over the Evo, um was that because it was slightly less explosive and not as quick, uh particularly to shoot to 12, is that I would wager many progressing riders would have an easier time consistently hitting the sweet spot on the Vortex for better vertical jumps. Now, over a full session, it's likely they would have one or two outlier jumps going higher on the Evo, but I have a suspicion on many um more jumps, they would consistently go as high or higher on the Vortex, particularly when trying tricks that are on the edge of their skill set. You could certainly make a good argument that the more controllable power of the Vortex would also likely be more confidence-boosting for big air tricks and progression. Now, before we get on to looping, I think I just need to mention and once again, the real highlight of this kite, like kites like the Evo or other three-strut Alula kites like the Slingshot NXT, is just what you get in all wind ranges from the low end to the top end in the power department. And I can remember occasions now with each of these kites where other riders were going out on their 10-m Dacron kites like the Arrows or Orbits, and I was able to get away with riding one of these three-strut Alula kites, be it the NXT, Evo, or recently with this Vortex, and still be able to jump similar heights and pull off similar tricks. Just such a bonus to be able to go down a kite size despite being a heavier rider. Turning to looping, once again, a very strong showing as you'd expect from the Vortex. However, when you add more power and lift, that is always going to come at a cost somewhere, and in this case, at least compared to the previous model, the loops are going to get slightly more powered, and again, a slightly fuller looping motion. Unless, of course, you really crank the bar a little bit more, making them require a little bit more technical skills and piloting, and perhaps some added confidence to go for them. The real joy of the older model for all level of riders, but more so the progressing ones with their first loops, was that it looped high and tight with very little pull, like your Orbit or Nitro style kites. But, as you progressed and started adding tricks to the loop, it still allowed you a very easy, low-risk loop. Sure, you could make the case that the loop was a little bit fast, so I do think there is an argument that this new model's stability and predictable loop may be beneficial to riders who have already gotten over the hump of their initial loops and are looking to progress into loops with more technical aspects to them or height. Um as more experienced loopers, my friends and I certainly felt like we enjoyed the more recent model in the looping department because since our review of that first Vortex 2 years ago, we've gotten to ride and probably gotten more used to a lot more powerful kites. And what the added power brings to the equation of the new Vortex is certainly for us worth a slight toll in the ease of use when it comes to looping. When comparing to the latest model Evo, we found the newer Vortex loop was still the tighter, softer pull and friendlier of the kites and certainly more confidence inspiring to loop. However, by comparison to the older model Evo D-Lab, at least in the 12 m size, we were riding them back-to-back, the Vortex was ever so slightly more challenging for me. Um but you could attribute this to my familiarity with the older Evos having been on them for 3 years now. In any case, both 12s are excellent loopers for the size. So, with those improvements in boosting but slight added challenges in looping, how would I rate the new Vortex in terms of confidence boosting? Well, a little bit of this is really going to depend on your level of course because one of the joys of the older Vortex was how a rider at my level could have so much fun on it, but then I could happily give it to my wife who is still a progressing rider just building her jumps and both of us would love the kite for our respective levels. Now, I still think a lot of that is carried over into the newer model, but I will say that the added performance in general would potentially come at a slight cost to a less experienced rider not as used to more powerful performance kites. And in the larger sizes, say 10 or 11, it probably wouldn't be quite as significant to adapt to because those kites are always going to be slower anyways. For me personally, I certainly think this trade-off is worthwhile because I would never usually recommend beginners and progressing riders just looking to get into loops to jump on such expensive high-end kites when really there are so many better, cheaper, practical models for them to progress on the marketplace. But of course, you know, if you have more money than skills, like I usually tend to do, why not? Go for a kite like this that can do a bit of everything. What I really like about the new model is that they have just done a great job overall of improving that power while still keeping the kite very nicely balanced in every aspect of its performance. What that means is that you just feel so much of the kite whether you're on the water or in the air and the amount of pressure you have to put into the bar to get a response meshes nicely with the action the kite takes as you engage it. Um and the bar power coming off the water is impressive without being over the top intimidating and the loops are although slightly more powered than the older model, still very friendly and easy to gain confidence in. I certainly felt like this kite would help me progress with all of my current big air tricks and goals despite at the time of this review I'm still recovering from a rib injury which prevented me from going any going for anything too challenging or on the edge of my skills. It's also great there is another three-strut Aluula option in all sizes that offer so much overall performance and is again another low V option. If I was still an orbit era or other Dacron kite user who rides low V kites, then I'd certainly be one to consider getting one of these kites in the larger sizes as it does offer so much more wind range and opportunities to kite and would likely be better value for money as an upgrade than in the smaller sizes for some people which you wouldn't likely get to ride as much as this one. Uh particularly say an 11 or 12 m where you can work on all your big air and still probably get some loops in. So, in summary, this kite is the logical and desirable upgrade from one of the already better kites on the market and should be very desirable to all those of Vortex riders who have already seen significant improvements in their riding since getting on the original version. Now, perhaps if they are still working on their first kite loops, then start with an upgrade in the larger sizes where it won't be as much of a factor. If you found this review enjoyable or helpful at all, please say so in the comments and be sure to like and subscribe and check out my Instagram for more up-to-date content that will show you what I'm currently working on. I've already begun editing a few other reviews, so the next month should be great for content so long as my regular workload allows me enough editing time. As always, thank you for making it this far and may all your local spots be windy. Until the next time, goodbye.

reviews.summary: Kitemana's riders compared the Vortex V2 with the Dacron Reflex. The Vortex felt stiffer, more direct and more powerful, with 15–20m jumps and loops once the wind picked up, but more sensitive to small steering mistakes and at its best with plenty of wind.

structured_review.summary: A clear step up from the original Vortex: more low end, more sheet-and-go lift and better stability, and it boosts within 5–10% of the Evo D/LAB while being easier to time. The added power brings heavier steering and a fuller, pulling loop, so it is less of a first-loop kite than V1.
pros: Excellent low end and wind range from the Aluula 3-strut frame
More power and sheet-and-go lift than the V1
Very stable in the air, which helps rotations and board-offs
Boost height close to the Evo D/LAB but easier to hit consistently
Lets heavier riders drop a size versus Dacron kites
cons: Heavier steering pressure and slightly slower response than V1
Fuller loop with more pull; less friendly for first loops
Stable 8-point bridle makes quick in-air kite moves take more effort
Felt unbalanced on a high-Y or light bar; wants a wide, heavier low-V bar
structured_review.best_for: Intermediate to advanced big air riders who want Aluula wind range with a controllable, confidence-building boost.
structured_review.not_for: Riders still learning their first kiteloops, or anyone on a light high-Y bar.
structured_review.rec_blurb: More power, same balance: a low-V Aluula booster that is easy to time.
